articles.title: Rising fuel prices another blow to Chicago restaurants
articles.text:
Rising fuel prices another blow to Chicago restaurants - WBEZ Chicago
Kevin Vaughan of Vaughan Hospitality stands behind the bar at Moon Star Kitchen & Bar, 1617 N. Wells St., in Old Town.
Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times
Economy
Rising fuel prices another blow to Chicago restaurants
Higher diesel prices are driving up food and supply costs for restaurants, as budget-conscious customers also cut back on dining out.
By
Misha Manjuran Oberoi
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Chicago restaurants are being squeezed from all sides as surging fuel prices drive up the cost of food and supplies, while higher household costs are prompting consumers to eat out less.
Several food suppliers have significantly raised their fuel surcharges, an added fee for clients to help cover fuel costs, as diesel prices climb amid the war in Iran. The average price of diesel in Chicago was $6.86 per gallon on Friday, up more than 68% from a year earlier, according to AAA. Diesel prices in the city reached its highest average price of $7.02 on Sept. 26.
“Everything we do comes in on trucks, right? All our supplies come in on trucks,” said Kevin Vaughan, owner of Vaughan Hospitality Group, which owns six bars and restaurants across Chicago, including Chicago Brewhouse and Corcoran’s Grill & Pub. “For example, food — beef, produce, etc. — there’s a huge impact on those industries because diesel is up so high and transport is up so high. So we’re starting to see that accelerate.”
Vaughan’s suppliers have said their freight charges are going up dramatically and will continue to be passed onto restaurants. One of his suppliers charges a $9 fuel surcharge when diesel costs $5 to $5.49 per gallon. Every time diesel increases by 50 cents, the supplier increases the surcharge by $1.
Vaughan also believes consumer demand is falling as higher gas prices squeeze household budgets.
“This is anecdotal, but I feel as if people are not necessarily going out as often … and [it’s] all driven by fuel and other things like interest rates, the cost to rent, etc.,” Vaughan said. “The consumer is feeling big pressure on managing their budgets.”
A KPMG survey from April found 67% of consumers are eating at home more often than dining out, with the majority citing budget concerns as the primary reason. When consumers do dine out, 25% said they’re frequenting quick-service or fast-food restaurants, shifting away from casual and fine dining options.
Mario Ponce, restaurant consultant with Chicago-based Partners in Hospitality, said he’s seeing a similar shift among his clients, with consumers trading casual sit-down restaurants for cheaper options such as fast-food, pizza and sandwich shops.
Ron Cain, owner of Kuma’s Corner, said sales at the burger restaurant are down 15% and 11% in the past four months, compared to the year before, for his Avondale and Schaumburg locations, respectively.
“Our Schaumburg location has been consistent since we opened in 2015, and this is the first year we’re really feeling an impact on the traffic,” Cain said.
Although sales are down, Kuma’s Corner is absorbing their cost increases, rather than passing them down to customers. These include rising beef prices due to the national cattle herd shortage, as well as suppliers’ fuel surcharges, Cain said.
But the trade-off is tricky. He said customer traffic is low, so raising prices might help, but it could reduce traffic further.
Kuma’s Corner at 2900 W. Belmont Ave.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times
“You can only charge so much for a burger,” Cain said. “So we have not passed down the cost of our margins.”
Instead, the restaurant is focusing on appealing to customers by offering temporary special deals and discounts that encourage them to dine out.
Some new offers include half-sized lunch burgers, mac and cheese and a beer for $12 on Mondays and a chicken sandwich with fries and a beer for $15 on Tuesdays. Kuma’s also launched a chicken caesar wrap on Sept. 1, which received 340 orders on DoorDash in the first month. Cain said they plan to sell the wrap with fries and a beer for $14.
“We’re doing that on a limited time basis, hoping that the economy’s going to turn around at some point, you know, hoping this war is going to end and the fuel prices are going to come down,” Cain said.
At Vaughan’s establishments, prices for beef menu items have increased while other costs are being absorbed by the company. Beef prices have squeezed his business the hardest, Vaughan said.
Fuel is also impacting the cost of plastic products, such as cups, since those are petroleum-based products, Vaughan said, adding another strain to his restaurants’ costs.
Sam Toia, president of the Illinois Restaurant Association, said small, independent and family-owned restaurants are particularly vulnerable because they have less buying power than larger restaurant chains and are seeing larger increases in fuel surcharges.
“If they were open six days a week, maybe they’re open five days a week,” Toia said. “If they’re open lunch and dinner, maybe they’re just open dinner … because the only two things you can control in the restaurant business is labor costs and food costs.”
Despite such measures, Toia feels restaurant closures will be inevitable if fuel prices remain high and economic pressures persist.
Cain is also worried.
“I mean, that’s my main concern — surviving all this nonsense,” Cain said.

articles.title: 1985 Bears championship team remembers former coach Mike Ditka as 'tip of the spear'
articles.text:
1985 Bears championship team remembers former coach Mike Ditka as 'tip of the spear' - WBEZ Chicago
FILE - Chicago Bears football coach Mike Ditka, watches from the sidelines during the Bears loss to the New England Patriots in an NFL football game in Foxboro, Mass., Nov. 2, 1988. (AP Photo/File) ORG XMIT: NYDD213
Anonymous/AP Photos
Sports
Politics
1985 Bears championship team remembers former coach Mike Ditka as 'tip of the spear'
Ditka led the Bears on an incredible five-year run in the 1980s, including the franchise’s only Super Bowl win. He died Friday at 86.
By
Jason Lieser
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Mike Ditka’s players have seemingly endless stories that capture the essence of who he was as a coach and a man. Those memories returned in a rush Friday when Ditka, who led the Bears to their only Super Bowl win and towered as a Chicago icon, died at 86.
Hall of Fame defensive lineman Dan Hampton’s snapshot might speak the loudest, especially as the Bears are set to visit the archrival Packers on Sunday.
The teams played a preseason game in 1984, and logistics were an issue since Milwaukee County Stadium was a baseball facility, so the Bears and Packers were on the same sideline. Ditka, of course, stood at one 49-yard line and Packers coach Forrest Gregg stood at the other, and Ditka spent the entire game screaming profanities at Gregg.
“He was the tip of the spear,” Hampton told the Sun-Times. “A lot of coaches say, ‘OK, do this, do this,’ and then they stand back and watch. Ditka was right there at the front.
“It was about us against you. Our team against you. Let’s go. It didn’t matter that it was preseason.”
Ditka coached the Bears to a five-year run as the NFL’s most powerful force as they went 62-17 from 1984 through ’88, the peak being his 1985 team that won Super Bowl XX. It is the only Lombardi Trophy in franchise history, and no coach since has matched his dominance.
That includes his sparkling 15-5 record against the Packers, whom the Bears visit Sunday.
He despised them. As good as Ditka was for the Bears as a tight end from 1961 through ’66, they ran up against the Packers during the Bart Starr era. Ditka went 3-9 against them as a player and never let go of that grudge.
“The whole City of Chicago hated the Packers, and he had played against all those legendary Packers teams and they beat up the Bears pretty good,” left tackle Jimbo Covert said. “There was a lot of animosity there, and he carried it forward. When you got to Green Bay week, you knew there was going to be more intensity on the practice field.”
It’s hard to imagine what that level must’ve been for Ditka, who was always at full throttle anyway.
Playing for him was grueling, so much so that Hall of Fame linebacker Mike Singletary referred to him as “a real badass,” but it brought out their best. They learned the value of preparation, worked relentlessly and adopted his ferocity.
“I didn’t realize how wonderful it was to be able to play for him until years after I retired,” Hampton said. “Nothing felt better than if we were playing against the 49ers and we’d go out and execute and beat their ass, and then come into the locker room and he was like a proud father.”
Ditka coached the Bears from 1982 through ’92, the longest tenure other than franchise founder George Halas, and went 106-62. He matched Halas’ team record with six playoff wins.
As a star tight end for the Bears, he helped them win the 1963 championship, made the Pro Bowl his first five seasons and still ranks in the top six all time in catches (316), yards receiving (4,503) and touchdown catches (34).
His brash playing style translated perfectly to coaching. His attitude rippled through the Bears as he established not only rigorous practice and preparation habits — “It was all about winning,” Hampton said — but the confidence that no one could stop them.
“We embraced the bravado that he displayed and the way he would just put it out there that we’re good and we know we’re good and you can’t do nothing about it,” said cornerback Leslie Frazier, now an assistant coach with the Seahawks. “That was rare, but that’s how he was. He took it personal if someone felt like they were better than us or tried to impose their will against us.”
Players knew of Ditka’s declining health the last few years, and Hampton wanted one last chance to see him. He stopped by last month, and while reality set in that his beloved coach didn’t have much longer, he got one last glimpse of the man he remembered in his prime.
“He wasn’t in the best of shape, but when I leaned over to look at him in the eyes, his eyes burned with that Ditka fire and he said, ‘Dan!’” Hampton said. “It was great.”
He was tough, but loving. And most of all, he was theirs.

articles.title: Mayor Johnson, Trump, Obama remember football 'titan' Mike Ditka
articles.text:
Mayor Johnson, Trump, Obama remember football 'titan' Mike Ditka - WBEZ Chicago
President Barack Obama is presented with a team jersey by former Bears’ head coach Mike Ditka as he stands with the 1985 Super Bowl XX Champions Chicago Bears NFL football team during a ceremony at the White House Oct. 7, 2011.
Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP
Sports
Politics
Mayor Johnson, Trump, Obama remember football 'titan' Mike Ditka
Former President Barack Obama said Ditka “set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant and fun.”
By
Violet Miller
Updated
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Hours before the Willis Towers’ antennas were set to light up in Bears blue and orange to honor Mike Ditka, whose death was announced Friday morning, Mayor Brandon Johnson acknowledged Ditka’s family, the city and “all who love Iron Mike.”
“Today, we lost a titan of the game and a hero of Chicago,” Johnson wrote in a statement on social media. “Mike Ditka revolutionized football and delivered glory to our great city on and off the field.”
He was among the dozens of political officials taking to social media to celebrate Ditka’s life.
Former President Barack Obama posted his own message on X with a photo of himself and Ditka holding up a Bears jersey emblazoned with Obama and the number 85 during a 2011 ceremony honoring the 1985 Super Bowl team at the White House.
The team’s original trip to the White House to meet Ronald Reagan had been scrapped following the explosion of the Challenger space shuttle that year.
Obama said that when he arrived in Chicago in 1985, Ditka and the championship team “were king.” It was high praise from a man Ditka once called the “ worst president we’ve ever had” while voicing his support for President Donald Trump and former president Ronald Reagan.
“Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it,” Obama wrote on social media. “I’m thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a legend.”
When I got to Chicago in the summer of 1985, Mike Ditka and the Chicago Bears were king. Coach Ditka set the tone for a team that was punishing, dominant, and fun — and the city loved him for it. I'm thinking of the Ditka family and Bears fans everywhere on the passing of a… pic.twitter.com/RKlJsahYbR— Barack Obama (@BarackObama) October 9, 2026
Trump, who was informed of Ditka’s passing during a news briefing Friday, said the late coach was “great” while touting his support while he was alive.
“He was a great guy,” Trump told reporters. “He was with me all the way. He was tough. That’s a sad one.”
Illinois officials posted their own tributes to “da coach,” as U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin called him in his message. Durbin, who announced last year that he would step down after five terms in the U.S. Senate and seven terms in the U.S. House, said Ditka coached with “style, grace, and respect for the game.”
“No Bears fan will ever forget the day when the Monsters of the Midway triumphed over the New England Patriots in Super Bowl XX,” Durbin said in a social media post. “Loretta and I will be praying for his family, friends, and former players as well as the millions of Chicagoans and Bears fans in mourning.”
Gov. JB Pritzker wrote on social media that “Da Coach was not only an icon in Chicago, but the entire football world. Our thoughts are with Mike Ditka’s family, friends, and Bears fans today. May his memory be a blessing.”
“Few people are as synonymous with Chicago as Mike Ditka,” Sen. Tammy Duckworth said in her own statement on social media. “Illinois will miss him dearly, but his legacy will never be forgotten. My heart goes out to his family and everyone who loved Da Coach.”
Longtime political consultant and former Obama advisor David Axelrod also expressed condolences for Ditka while sharing a story of filming a political campaign ad with him for former Chicago Mayor Richard M. Daley.
“When he popped in to do the spot, I started to explain what we were going for,” Axelrod wrote. “He looked at me with a withering stare and said, ‘Just turn on the F-ing camera. I know what I want to say.’ He always did.”

articles.title: Mike Ditka inspired comedic gold. But the funniest riff was Ditka as Ditka.
articles.text:
Mike Ditka inspired comedic gold. But the funniest riff was Ditka as Ditka. - WBEZ Chicago
Chicago Bears football coach Mike Ditka chats with Johnny Carson during a taping of “The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson,” Jan. 20, 1987.
Mark Avery/ASSOCIATED PRESS
Arts & Culture
Sports
Mike Ditka inspired comedic gold. But the funniest riff was Ditka as Ditka.
How could you script somebody more alpha, more intense, more intimidating, more hilarious and more memorable than the real Mike Ditka?
By
Richard Roeper
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Mike Ditka could bowl over a linebacker, make a sensational catch, motivate his players to greatness, dress down a reporter, out-heckle a heckler, sell you a refrigerator, coach “The Refrigerator,” and make an entire city laugh without ever telling a joke.
And then he’d have a cigar.
While Mike Ditka’s primary and iconic legacy as a football player and coach is celebrated elsewhere on these pages, let’s also give Ditka his due as a personality and a performer who starred in dozens of local and national commercials, appeared on “Saturday Night Live” and “Cheers,” and proved to be a worthy comedic partner to Will Ferrell on the big screen.
This list of football greats turned actors is extensive and impressive, from Jim Brown and Alex Karras to Don Meredith to Merlin Olsen, from Dick Butkus to Fred Dryer, from Terry Bradshaw to Peyton Manning to Nnamdi Asomugha. But whereas we could buy into Jim Brown playing Robert Jefferson in “The Dirty Dozen,” or Fred Dryer as “Hunter” and Merlin Olsen as “Father Murphy,” or even Peyton Manning as Coach Gary on “Modern Family,” Ditka almost always played Ditka.
On rare occasions, Ditka portrayed a fictional character — for example, “Coach Mafferty” on a couple of episodes of “3rd Rock from the Sun” in 1997, and the mayor of Chicago in a Make-A-Wish Foundation short film project called “Madzilla!” in 2014 — but from episodes of “L.A. Law,” “Coach,” “Becker” and “Entourage,” among other series, the coach played a lightly fictionalized version of himself, and invariably stole the scene.
It made sense. Ditka was just going to swallow any character whole anyway. How could you script somebody more alpha, more intense, more intimidating, more complicated, more hilarious and more memorable than the real Mike Ditka?
Mike Ditka as himself and coach Phil Weston (Will Ferrell) in the 2005 movie “Kicking and Screaming.”
Provided
The coach was a Hall of Fame presence in TV ads, from local spots for rustproofers and car dealerships to national spots for products too numerous to mention, including a memorable Super Bowl ad when he donned Packers gear and Jerry Rice wore Cowboys merch. (One of my favorites: the 1988 “Calling Me Home, Chicago” tourism ad, with Butkus returning home and surprising Ditka at Butch McGuire’s, and the two exchange the simplest and most profound greetings: “Butkus.” “Ditka.” Pure gold.)
Unscripted Ditka was also magnificently unpredictable, whether he was heckling back at hecklers at press conferences or on sports talk radio, donning roller skates and barreling through the Bears’ offices after dubbing Minnesota’s old indoor arena “The Rollerdome,” or racing through “Take Me Out to the Ballgame” at Wrigley Field in a land-speed record of 22 seconds in 1998.
The most complete meta-Ditka performance came in the 2005 comedy “Kicking and Screaming,” in which Will Ferrell’s quintessential suburban dad, Phil Weston, recruits Ditka to be the assistant coach for Phil’s son’s youth soccer team. It’s a fully realized role, with Ditka leaning into his hot-tempered persona to mine tremendous laughs. (In our two thumbs up review of the film on “Ebert & Roeper,” I said Ditka deserved a sitcom deal based on this performance; Roger noted, “Ditka is playing himself, and playing himself as nobody else could, and he gets laughs out of just turning and looking at Will Ferrell.”)
On a personal note, I had the privilege of narrating a live reading of the unproduced “Superfans” movie script written by Robert Smigel and Bob Odenkirk, the creators of that legendary series of sketches. In an Instagram post on Friday, Smigel told the story of 2001 ESPN roast of Ditka where Ditka eschewed the traditional rebuttal: “The whole event was a benefit for Misericordia, a residence where … children and adults with intellectual disabilities are provided personalized care … Coach Ditka used his time to talk about … what Misericordia provides. He could’ve gotten huge laughs firing back at all of us but he cared much more about Misericordia.”
The live reading of “Da Bears Movie Dat Wasn’t” was staged at the Park West in June of 2010, with performers including Smigel, Odenkirk, George Wendt, Joe Mantegna, David Koechner, my Sun-Times colleague Rick Telander, Keith Van Horne and Ryan Dempster — but it was Dikta as Ditka who stole the show.
As he did every time.

articles.title: Mary Ellen Guest, who headed the Chicago Bungalow Association, dies at 71
articles.text:
Mary Ellen Guest, who headed the Chicago Bungalow Association, dies at 71 - WBEZ Chicago
Mary Ellen Guest
Provided
Obituaries
Housing
Mary Ellen Guest, who headed the Chicago Bungalow Association, dies at 71
She focused on expanding membership in underserved communities and headed the ‘Stop the Pop’ campaign, which targeted roof renovations that compromised the signature look of the Chicago bungalow.
By
Mitch Dudek
[month] [day], [year], [hour]:[minute][ampm] [timezone]
SHARE
COPY LINK
Share
Email
Facebook
Twitter
Bluesky
Print
Mary Ellen Guest made sure the mission of the Chicago Bungalow Association, as much as it was about the brick-and-mortar gems central to the city’s DNA, was really about the people who lived in them.
Before she was hired as executive director in 2008, the non-profit centered on celebrating and preserving the unique architectural style of Chicago bungalows, which account for a third of the city’s single family housing stock.
“Mary Ellen transformed our mission to focus on the people who live in the bungalows,” said Gillian Wineman, deputy director of the association.
North Side bungalows in 2009. The architectural style accounts for a third of the city’s single family housing stock.
Tom Cruze/Sun-Times file
“She took the white gloves of preservation off. She made preservation practical and accessible, helping homeowners get what they needed to stay in their homes and make them safer, more comfortable, and affordable to live in,” Wineman said.
Ms. Guest died Sept. 20 from health complications following a fall. She was 71.
The association, which receives part of its funding from the city, was created by Mayor Richard M. Daley (who grew up in a bungalow) in 2000 to help preserve and maintain the city’s iconic homes. It has more than 68,000 members.
“She really had the ability to connect on an individual level with members and understand their true needs, and she always stayed true to her “meet you where you are” approach,” said Wineman, who is serving as interim executive director.
Membership, which is free, nearly quadrupled under Ms. Guest’s watch.
Ms. Guest was especially proud of focusing membership growth in underserved communities on the South and West Sides.
She attended up to 80 events a year in spaces ranging from church basements to community centers to spread the word about the many ways the non-profit could help with things like connecting homeowners to energy efficiency programs, trusted contractors and funding sources.
She also expanded the scope of the association’s mission to include older homes that were not bungalows.
“Everybody she worked with loved her, and she was tireless, she’d work all day at their office in the Monadnock Building and then be beating the drum out in the community,” said Tom Murphy, a founding board member of the association.
“For better or worse home ownership is the path to wealth building in this country and has been for a long time and Mary Ellen took pride in helping steer resources to working-class neighborhoods to preserve housing stock,” said Chris Meister, a longtime friend who serves as auditor general of the state of Illinois.
Ms. Guest also oversaw a “Stop the Pop” campaign that began in 2016 against “pop top” expansions of bungalows — so named because they “pop” off the lower roof of a bungalow and replace it with a much larger, usually squared-off, second floor.
The group believes the approach sacrifices the quintessential look of a bungalow for the sake of space.
To change minds, they offered two preferred alternatives to second floor additions that emphasize thoughtful design but cost about the same, if not less, than a full “pop.”
The campaign marked just how far appreciation for the bungalow had come. When the association was founded, bungalows were unfashionable and “thought of as your grandma’s house,” Guest told the Sun-Times in 2018.
When she took the helm, the group’s title was the “Historic Chicago Bungalow Association.” Ms. Guest lopped off the word “Historic” to emphasize its active and forward-thinking mission.
But she made sure paying homage to the history of the bungalow remained key, overseeing an expansion of National Register Bungalow Historic Districts in the city.
Ms. Guest was born Aug 3, 1955, to Ronald and Helen Guest. He was a dispatcher for a trucking company. She worked as a medical librarian for a hospital.
Ms. Guest grew up on the Southwest Side and attended the now-closed Queen of Peace High School and earned an education degree from Chicago State University.
In 1982 she got into political campaign work, starting as a volunteer and working her way up to head the campaign office for Adlai Stevenson III’s unsuccessful 1982 gubernatorial campaign.
She worked on a number of other campaigns, including Richard M. Daley’s unsuccessful mayoral run in 1983 and his first two successful mayoral campaigns in 1989 and 1991, for which she became known as the “Queen of the Phone Banks” by recruiting and organizing hundreds of volunteers to work the phones.
She later served as executive director of Working in the Schools, a Chicago non-profit that promotes literacy, and A+ Illinois, a coalition that advocated for equitable school funding reform.
“She was such a positive and wonderfully warmhearted person who served as a mentor to lots of people and really was like the glue who got people to stick together and work together on things,” said friend and political strategist Pete Giangreco, who worked in the campaign trenches with Ms. Guest.
“And she was a force,” he said. “You didn’t want to be on the other side of a righteously indignant Mary Ellen.”
Ms. Guest loved baking, her Irish heritage, attending the South Side Irish parade and her two sons whom she raised as a single mother in the Beverly area.

articles.title: Reopened probe into CPS Board president candidate’s alleged inappropriate contact with teen could end soon
articles.text:
Reopened probe into CPS Board president candidate’s alleged inappropriate contact with teen could end soon - WBEZ Chicago
Hilario Dominguez is one of three candidates running to become the first elected school board president in Chicago. He’s had to contend with the resurfacing of 2017 allegations against him.
Victor Hilitski/For the Sun-Times
Education
Elections
Chicago School Board
Reopened probe into CPS Board president candidate’s alleged inappropriate contact with teen could end soon
CPS’ inspector general reopened an investigation involving a former CPS student and Hilario Dominguez, the teachers union-backed candidate. The woman says she’s looking for accountability. Dominguez denies any wrongdoing and questions why the 2017 allegations resurfaced during a heated race. Election Day is Nov. 3.
By
Sarah Karp

The Chicago Public Schools’ inspector general could soon issue findings in its recently reopened investigation into whether Hilario Dominguez, a candidate for Chicago School Board president, acted inappropriately with a 17-year-old in 2017.
Investigators interviewed the woman, who is now 26, in late September and reinterviewed Dominguez on Tuesday.
The woman told the Chicago Tribune and other media outlets that Dominguez asked about her dating life while they were alone in a car, and he once lifted her up in a hug and spun her around. At the time, Dominguez was 24 and an organizer at The Resurrection Project, a Pilsen-based nonprofit, while she was a CPS student working there through the city’s summer jobs program.
The woman told Chalkbeat and Block Club Chicago that the hug with her body pressed against his made her feel “very uncomfortable” and that the car interaction was “really alarming” because Dominguez “was a figure of authority that I trusted.” She also said the concerning behavior stopped after she complained to an adult staffer.
The young woman has personal ties to Dominguez’s former political rival, Aida Flores, according to several sources. Dominguez denies the allegations and says they are politically motivated.
“For me, this is beyond a political campaign,” he told WBEZ. “This is about how I hold my head up high in the neighborhoods and in the city that raised me.”
The school district’s watchdog first opened an investigation into the alleged incidents in 2021 when Dominguez was teaching in CPS. He left that position in 2022 to work as deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, which endorsed Dominguez in the school board race.
Earlier this year, the inspector general’s office determined the allegations were unsubstantiated, according to an email sent by an investigator to Dominguez reviewed by WBEZ. But the office recently reopened the case.
Inspector General Philip Wagenknecht would not comment on why, but the woman told the Tribune that she reached out to his office because she was not interviewed for the original investigation.
These accusations have been thrust into Chicago’s heated school board president contest.
Jessica Biggs, one of Dominguez’s opponents in the race, said the alleged conduct was “deeply concerning” and that women and girls in CPS are paying attention.
“They deserve to know that the next leader of the CPS Board of Education will take their experiences seriously,” she said.
One of Biggs’ staffers, Alaina Hampton, said in a statement that she has known the woman for years and was long aware of the allegations. Hampton said the woman reached out to her in early September when the inspector general informed her the case was closed. Hampton recommended the woman hire a lawyer. Hampton said she would “continue to stand in solidarity with victims and survivors.”
Hampton was part of a high-profile sexual harassment lawsuit filed in 2018 against the Democratic Party of Illinois and others. She settled that case.
Through her lawyer, the woman declined to respond to questions from WBEZ. But she has said she is speaking out now because she wanted to tell her own story. She told NBC Chicago that Dominguez’s interactions with her should disqualify him from serving as school board president.
People gathered during a press conference outside The Resurrection Project in 2023. A woman alleges that Hilario Dominguez acted inappropriately with her when she worked at the Pilsen-based nonprofit through a summer jobs program in 2017.
Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times file
Dominguez left the Resurrection Project in 2018 to run for alderperson of the 25th Ward. Flores, an assistant principal at CPS, was one of four opponents.
Dominguez says these allegations first surfaced during that race. They both lost.
When Flores ran a second time in 2023, she was backed by a political action committee that opposes the CTU. Flores’ campaign website says she’s collecting petitions to run again in February.
Flores said in an email to WBEZ that she would not discuss the matter while the inspector general’s investigation was ongoing. Earlier this week, Flores told Chalkbeat and Block Club that she was not involved in surfacing the allegations.
Dominguez insists “that he did not have those types of interactions” with the woman.
He also said that he believes sexual misconduct should be taken seriously.
Paloma Rodriguez, a former housing coordinator for The Resurrection Project, told WBEZ that she sent emails in 2017 telling senior management that the young woman felt uncomfortable around Dominguez.
When Dominguez announced he was running for office in 2018, she said she decided to become “louder” about the alleged behavior. She submitted an official report to senior management in December 2018, according to a redacted copy reviewed by WBEZ. Rodriguez told WBEZ she also wrote it to “cover her butt” and preserve the information.
